name: Digital Compact Cassette audio format
summary: Philips's Digital Compact Cassette, on sale from October 1992, recorded compressed digital audio on cassette tape yet still played ordinary analogue cassettes; consumer production ended in 1996.
description: A digital magnetic-tape audio format using a stationary multichannel thin-film head and lossy PASC compression, with playback compatibility for earlier analogue Compact Cassettes.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

impact.note: A consumer tape format with few buyers, a variant of existing digital recording, abandoned in four years; implies tier 3, two below the reviewed tier 1.

why: Philips wanted a digital successor to its Compact Cassette that could still play buyers' existing tapes, as rival digital formats appeared.

market.note: A documented market offering or sale demonstrates applicability without proving the first global transaction.

events.statement: A contemporary UK report says Digital Compact Cassette equipment went on sale in October 1992.
events.scope: Consumer DCC recorder/player capable of reading existing analogue Compact Cassettes and recording DCC.
events.caveats: The exact first transaction is unknown. Sharp’s 1983 CX-3 prototype already made digital recordings on ordinary Compact Cassettes with a stationary 18-track head and 14-bit 44.1 kHz stereo PCM; its ability to play pre-existing analogue recordings is not established here. DCC combined lossy 384 kbit/s PASC coding, nine tracks per direction and analogue-recording playback: lower-rate coding trades exact sample preservation for compression. This is not a claim of first compatibility, demonstrated cost savings or universal sound superiority. Marketed rotary-head DAT and recordable MiniDisc used different mechanisms. Ordinary analogue tapes were not DCC digital recording media.

evidence.supports: The manufacturers describe thin-film stationary heads, nine tracks, 384 kbit/s PASC and analogue-cassette playback.
